To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have developed a new algorithm for estimating stellar metallicities and distances based on photometric measurements from the Canada-French-Imaging-Surveys, Pan-STARRS and Gaia, which we have applied to approximately 12 million stellar candidates in the northern sky.
we have developed an algorithm that can identify dwarf and giant stars, and estimate their distances and metallicity, with a high success rate.

we have developed an efficient algorithm that can be applied to photometry to estimate the distances, metallicities, and stellar types of stars out to a distance $R \sim 80$~kpc, which will enable studies of the outer disc and the Galactic halo.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions.
the development of new algorithms for the identification of stars in photometric data, and their application to the study of the Milky Way's external components.
the study of the chemical and dynamical structure of our Galaxy and its outer components.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the algorithm is a very promising and powerful tool to identify and characterize the stellar populations in the outer disc and the Galactic halo.

the CFHT Legacy Survey (CFHTLS) is a very successful project, which has delivered a large amount of excellent data, and that the CFHTLS Wide Survey has provided the scientific community with a unique dataset.
the CFHTLS is a great instrument for the study of galaxies and clusters.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have created an algorithm that is fully data-driven and that is capable of identifying dwarfs and giants, and estimating the distance and metallicity for a significant number of stars in the CFIS/PS1/Gaia footprint.
we have developed a novel algorithm that is able to identify dwarf stars from giants and to estimate the distances of the latter.

we have developed a new algorithm for the identification of dwarf and giant stars in the Galaxy, and we have applied it to the CFIS/PS1/Gaia data to produce the first catalogue of distances and metallicities for a large sample of stars out to $\sim 80$kpc.
The main takeaway from our work is that

photometry alone can be used to discriminate between dwarf stars and giant stars and estimate their metallicities and distances, thus enabling studies that would have been impossible to perform otherwise.
it is possible to estimate distances to stars in the outer disc and the halo of the Milky Way with a high degree of precision, and to discriminate between dwarf stars and giants.
photometric stellar parameters can be estimated to a high degree of accuracy using data from current and future surveys.
